algorithm: Use the purely inductive infinite bus from Section II-B. At no load, i_d0 = i_q0 = 0. The perturbation states are the power angle and the d- and q-axis currents.
Conventional PSC uses ξ = 0. RFPSC uses ξ = 1 and feeds ΔP_ref / V into the active-resistance branch. Both variants use the same feedback gain K_p.
Integrate the dq perturbation equations and the transfer-function implementation of Eq. (19) with RK4. Compare RFPSC with the no-load solution 1 − exp(−ατ) and repeat with half the step size.
strengths: In the strong-grid example with L = 0.1 p.u., the 10–90% rise time was 3.50 ms for RFPSC and 11.50 ms for conventional PSC.
All three no-load RFPSC traces matched the first-order analytical response. RFPSC eliminated the small overshoot seen with conventional PSC at L = 0.5 and 1.0 p.u.
limitations: The speed benefit depends on grid inductance. At L = 0.5 and 1.0 p.u., RFPSC eliminated overshoot and took longer to rise from 10% to 90%.

This run covers a balanced, purely inductive, no-load small-signal model. Approximate cancellation under load, finite filter bandwidth, sampling and PWM delay, current limiting and the hardware traces in Figs. 5–6 remain unverified.
